## Q4
Which of the following parser is most powerful parser?

## Q4 - Options
(A) Operator precedence
(B) SLR
(C) Canonical LR
(D) LALR

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q44

Among shift-reduce parsers, the LR parser family forms a strict power hierarchy. Canonical LR (LR(1)) can handle every grammar that SLR and LALR can, plus more, because it keeps a distinct lookahead set for every individual state-item pair instead of merging states. SLR and LALR are more restrictive since they merge states to save memory, which can introduce parsing conflicts that Canonical LR avoids. Operator precedence parsing is weaker still, working only for a narrow class of expression grammars. So Canonical LR is the most powerful parser of the four.

## Q5
Which phase of a compiler checks the grammar of the programming language?

## Q5 - Options
(A) Code optimization
(B) Semantic analysis
(C) Code generators
(D) Syntax analysis

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

Syntax analysis is the compiler phase that checks whether the sequence of tokens produced by lexical analysis conforms to the language's grammar, building a parse tree from the grammar's production rules.

- **A. Code optimization** — wrong phase. It improves already-generated intermediate code and does not check grammar.
- **B. Semantic analysis** — wrong phase. It checks meaning-level rules such as type compatibility, after the grammar has already been validated.
- **C. Code generators** — wrong phase. Code generation produces target-machine instructions from validated, optimized intermediate code.
- **D. Syntax analysis** — correct. It is the parsing phase that validates grammatical structure.

## Q6
While processing a string by an LR parser, the reading of the given string by the parser is--------------.

## Q6 - Options
(A) From right to left
(B) From left to right
(C) Can be either from left to right or right to left
(D) From the centre of the given string

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q31

An LR parser reads its input tokens strictly from left to right while building a rightmost derivation in reverse using a shift-reduce strategy.

The "L" in LR specifically refers to this left-to-right scanning direction, while the "R" refers to producing a rightmost derivation, so the parser never scans from the right, from the center, or in either direction interchangeably.

## Q7
Match List I with List II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Initial Configuration of stack and input in LL Parsing process | I. $ w$ |
| B. Final Configuration of stack and input in LL Parsing process | II. $ $ |
| C. Initial Configuration of stack and input in LR Parsing process | III. $S w$ |
| D. Final Configuration of stack and input in LR Parsing process | IV. $S $ |

## Q7 - Options
(A) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
(B) A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV
(C) A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
(D) A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q72

Top-down (LL) and bottom-up (LR) parsers start and end their stack contents in opposite ways, which fixes each configuration in this list.

An LL parser begins with the start symbol already predicted onto the stack (with the input still unread), giving stack-input configuration $S paired with w$, so the initial LL configuration is A-III.

An LL parser finishes successfully once the stack is reduced back to just the bottom marker and the input is fully consumed to just its end marker, giving $ paired with $, so the final LL configuration is B-II.

An LR parser instead begins with an empty stack (just the bottom marker) since it has not shifted or reduced anything yet, with the entire input still ahead, giving $ paired with w$, so the initial LR configuration is C-I.

An LR parser finishes successfully once it has reduced the entire input down to the start symbol on the stack, with the input consumed to its end marker, giving $S paired with $, so the final LR configuration is D-IV.

This gives the mapping A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

## Q8
The item generated by the production A → ε is:

## Q8 - Options
(A) A → •
(B) A → ε•
(C) A → •ε
(D) A → ε

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q31

An LR item marks how much of a production's right-hand side has already been seen with a dot, so for a normal production the dot sits between recognized and unrecognized symbols.

Because A → ε has an empty right-hand side, there are no symbols on either side of the dot to place it between, so the standard convention writes the single resulting item as A → • with the dot alone, omitting the ε symbol entirely rather than writing it out before or after the dot.

## Q9
Consider the following statements:<br>
Statement I: LALR parser is more powerful than canonical LR Parser.<br>
Statement II: SLR parser is more powerful than LALR<br>
Which of the following is correct?

## Q9 - Options
(A) Statement I true and Statement II false
(B) Statement I false and Statement II true
(C) Both Statement I and Statement II false
(D) Both Statement I and Statement II true

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q81

The standard power hierarchy among these LR-family parsers is LR(0) ⊆ SLR ⊆ LALR ⊆ canonical LR(1).

Statement I is false. Canonical LR is the most powerful of the four, strictly more powerful than LALR, not the other way around.<br>
Statement II is false. LALR is strictly more powerful than SLR, not less.

Both statements invert the actual hierarchy, so both are false.

## Q11

## Q11 - Options
(A) Syntax trees
(B) Three-address codes
(C) Quadruples
(D) Postfix notation

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q30

Three-address code, quadruples, and postfix notation are linear intermediate-code representations used in translation. A syntax tree is a structural representation of the parsed program rather than an intermediate code sequence.

A. Storage allocation<br>
B. Checking type compatibility<br>
C. Suppressing duplicate-error messages

## Q12 - Options
(A) (A) and (B) only

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** D

## Q13
On translating the expression given below into quadruple representation, how many operations are required?<br>
(i*j) + (e + f) \* (a*b + c)

## Q13 - Options
(A) 5
(B) 6
(C) 3
(D) 7

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q2

A quadruple representation specifies an operation using four fields: operator, argument 1, argument 2, and result.

Translating the arithmetic expression step by step generates six distinct operations:

1. t1 = i \* j
2. t2 = e + f
3. t3 = a \* b
4. t4 = t3 + c
5. t5 = t2 \* t4
6. t6 = t1 + t5

Each line corresponds to exactly one quadruple record, yielding 6 operations in total.

## Q14
Shift-reduce parser consists of<br>
(a) input buffer<br>
(b) stack<br>
(c) parse table

Choose the correct option from those give below:

## Q14 - Options
(A) (a) and (b) only
(B) (a) and (c) only
(C) (c) only
(D) (a), (b) and (c)

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q23

A shift-reduce bottom-up parser operates using three integral components:

- **(a) Input buffer** — stores the remaining input string terminated by an end marker ($).
- **(b) Stack** — maintains the shift-reduce state symbols and handles grammar reductions.
- **(c) Parse table** — guides the parser actions (shift, reduce, accept, error) and state transitions via ACTION and GOTO tables.

All three components are required.

## Q15
Which data structure is used by the compiler for managing variables and their attributes?

## Q15 - Options
(A) Binary tree
(B) Link list
(C) Symbol table
(D) Parse table

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q26

A symbol table is a central data structure created and maintained by compilers to store identifier records.

It tracks variable names, data types, scope levels, memory offsets, and binding attributes across lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic checking, and code generation phases.

- **A. Binary tree** — can be an underlying implementation for a symbol table, but is not the conceptual data structure itself.
- **B. Link list** — another possible implementation mechanism for symbol tables.
- **D. Parse table** — guides the syntax analyzer in choosing grammar production rules.

## Q16
The grammar S → (S) \| SS \| ε is not suitable for predictive parsing because the grammar is

## Q16 - Options
(A) An operator grammar
(B) Ambiguous
(C) Left recursive
(D) Right recursive

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q49

The grammar S → (S) \| SS \| ε generates balanced parentheses but is inherently ambiguous due to the production S → SS.

- For a string such as '()()()', multiple distinct leftmost derivations and parse trees can be generated.
- No ambiguous grammar can be parsed by an LL(1) predictive parser because ambiguity leads to multiple entries in the parsing table.
- The grammar is not left recursive because S does not appear as the immediate leftmost symbol of its own body without terminals.
- Therefore, ambiguity is the reason it cannot be used for predictive parsing (Option B).

## Q17
Consider the following grammar G :

S → A \| B<br>
A → a \| c<br>
B → b \| c

where {S, A, B}, the set of non-terminals, and {a, b, c}, the set of terminals.<br>
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct ?

S1 : LR(1) can parse all strings that are generated using grammar G.<br>
S2 : LL(1) can parse all strings that are generated using grammar G.

Choose the correct answer from the code given below :<br>
Code :

## Q17 - Options
(A) Neither S1 nor S2
(B) Only S1
(C) Only S2
(D) Both S1 and S2

## Q17 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Parsing, FIRST/FOLLOW, Compiler Phases & Three-Address Code
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q78

Grammar G is ambiguous because terminal string 'c' has two distinct leftmost derivations, preventing it from being parsed by any deterministic LL or LR parser.

- For string 'c', two derivations exist:
   
   1. S =&gt; A =&gt; c
   2. S =&gt; B =&gt; c
- Ambiguity introduces a FIRST/FIRST conflict in LL(1) parsers because FIRST(A) and FIRST(B) both contain terminal 'c'.
- Ambiguity introduces a reduce/reduce conflict in LR(1) parsers when lookahead symbol is end-of-input ($), because the parser cannot decide whether to reduce to non-terminal A or B.
- Because no ambiguous grammar can be LL(1) or LR(1), neither statement S1 nor S2 is correct (Option A).
